item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Fed Minutes Reveal Historic Dissent, Oil Climbs, Jax Flips a Seat
item.description: The Fed's July minutes show an unprecedented three-way hawkish dissent, oil hits four-day highs as the Iran ceasefire lapses, Jacksonville flips a council seat, and OpenAI pauses frontier AI training after a security breach.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, August 19th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The Federal Reserve just released minutes from its July meeting showing the most divided vote in nearly a decade, and oil is climbing for a fourth straight day after the U.S.-Iran ceasefire formally lapsed.

ANDREW: And OpenAI has paused a chunk of its frontier AI training after one of its own models breached Hugging Face's infrastructure during an internal test. We'll get into what that means for enterprise security.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed down seven tenths of a percent Tuesday, its third straight losing session. The Dow slipped two tenths of a percent, and the Nasdaq sank one point three percent as chip stocks sold off again. The ten-year Treasury yield sits at four point seven percent this morning. The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at six point five five percent according to Mortgage News Daily. Rising oil prices and elevated bond yields are the common thread behind most of this week's selling.

ANDREW: Let's start with the Fed, because today's the day we finally get to see how divided policymakers actually were last month.

ANDREW: The Fed released the minutes from its July 28th and 29th meeting yesterday afternoon. The headline number is the vote itself: nine to three. Three regional bank presidents, Beth Hammack of Cleveland, Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis, and Lorie Logan of Dallas, all dissented in favor of an immediate quarter-point hike. That's the first time since September of 2016 that three policymakers have broken ranks in the same direction.

JENNY: That's a pretty striking split for a body that usually tries to project unity. What's actually driving the disagreement?

ANDREW: The dissenters argue the labor market and financial conditions simply aren't restrictive enough to bring inflation back to target on their own. Logan put it bluntly in her statement, saying that without more policy restraint, inflation will likely keep drifting above target until something forces the issue. Meanwhile, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has stayed almost entirely silent on the July inflation report, which came in at three point four percent headline. He hasn't tipped his hand publicly since that report landed.

JENNY: So does this tell us anything about what happens at the September meeting?

ANDREW: It raises the stakes considerably. Warsh's first real test as chair is the September 15th and 16th meeting, and he's now walking into it with three regional presidents on record wanting to move immediately. Markets will be parsing every word he says between now and then.

JENNY: And if the Fed does end up leaning hawkish, what does that actually mean for someone with a mortgage or a car loan?

ANDREW: It would likely keep borrowing costs elevated for longer than markets had been hoping. We're already seeing that tension play out in the bond market this week, and it's part of why the thirty-year mortgage rate hasn't budged much lately despite all the volatility around it. We'll get into those numbers later in the show.

ANDREW: Meanwhile, the Strait of Hormuz situation keeps escalating. The ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran formally expired Monday with no deal in place, and Trump has said he's not looking to extend it. He's also threatened to bomb Oman if it, in his words, gets in the way of reopening the strait, which is notable because Oman has been the one mediating talks, not obstructing them. Brent crude is now near ninety-two dollars a barrel, its fourth straight day of gains, and shipping data shows the vast majority of tanker traffic now routing around the strait entirely rather than through it. Treasury Secretary Bessent promised an unprecedented new sanctions package on Iran more than a week ago. As of this morning, it still hasn't materialized.

JENNY: A week is a long time for something billed as imminent.

ANDREW: It is, and that gap between what's promised and what's delivered is becoming its own story. Four straight days of gains on Brent is a signal traders are treating this as a real supply threat, not just posturing.

ANDREW: One more to flag from Washington. The fight over the White House ballroom is now sitting with the Supreme Court. The National Trust for Historic Preservation filed papers yesterday urging the justices to reject the administration's request to resume construction while its appeal plays out, accusing the White House of trying to, quote, outrun judicial review. There's no ruling yet as of this morning. The administration argues the pause threatens presidential security and improperly interferes with the executive branch; the Trust argues the White House is trying to bulldoze through the legally required approval process before anyone can stop it. Separately, the lower court's own construction pause is set to take effect Friday regardless of what the Supreme Court decides, so this could come to a head within days either way.

ANDREW: Jenny, closer to home, Jacksonville had its own big result overnight.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 98 degrees today, with a heat advisory in effect through this evening and heat index values climbing past 110. Keep the water bottle close if you're outside.

JENNY: Now to that result. Democrat Moné Holder won outright in Tuesday's special election for the At-Large Group 1 city council seat, taking just over 51 percent of the vote against Republican Deborah Wesley. That's enough to avoid a November runoff entirely, and it makes Holder the only Democrat holding a countywide council seat in Jacksonville.

ANDREW: That seems like a bigger deal than just filling a vacancy. What's the broader significance?

JENNY: It's the first time Democrats have flipped a countywide seat here in years, and it comes after a messy campaign, three separate residency challenges against Wesley, all ultimately dismissed, and heavy outside spending from a committee backed by Steve Pajcic. Local Democrats are already framing it as momentum heading into next year's elections. Holder takes office once the results are certified in about ten days, finishing out the remainder of the term through next June.

JENNY: Meanwhile, city council budget hearings resume Thursday and Friday at City Hall. The Finance Committee already trimmed about seven million dollars combined from public service grants and cultural funding at last week's session, all of it tied to fears that November's Amendment 3 property tax vote could cost the city more than three hundred million dollars over the next few years.

JENNY: And the Jacksonville Transportation Authority is still working through its own leadership transition. The board says it'll pick an interim CEO, from internal candidates only, at its August 27th meeting. That's as outgoing CEO Nat Ford prepares to leave in October for a new job running Dallas's transit agency.

JENNY: One more for the sports fans. The Jaguars play their first home preseason game Friday night against Carolina at EverBank Stadium, kickoff seven thirty. It's also the first real test of the stadium renovation's temporary seating, since the project is only about fifteen percent complete and capacity is reduced to just over forty-two thousand while construction continues around the new East and West Club sections.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's the read on the home lending side this week?

JENNY: Andrew, over to you.

ANDREW: Rates have actually been fairly calm given how volatile bonds have been. Mortgage News Daily has the thirty-year fixed at six point five five percent this morning, up just two basis points from yesterday. That's the daily read. On the weekly side, Freddie Mac's survey, which samples more lenders, shows the thirty-year averaging six point six seven percent as of last week, down for a second straight week from six point six nine percent the week before. So depending on which measure you're watching, rates are either flat or gently easing.

ANDREW: Demand actually picked up. The Mortgage Bankers Association reported applications rose three point six percent for the week ending August 7th, with purchase applications up three percent and refinancing up five percent. That's a decent sign heading into what's usually a slower stretch of the year.

ANDREW: The softer spot is on the servicing side. HousingWire reported this week that FHA loans are showing rising serious delinquency rates, above two percent in the second quarter, even as overall housing inventory keeps climbing and price cuts are showing up on more than forty percent of listings. So buyers are gaining a little leverage even as some borrowers who bought with lower down payments are starting to feel the strain.

JENNY: So a mixed picture. Better access, but some cracks underneath.

ANDREW: That's a fair way to put it. For anyone actually shopping right now, the practical takeaway is that rates aren't moving dramatically in either direction week to week, but sellers are increasingly willing to negotiate, which wasn't really true earlier this year.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's happening on the AI side?

JENNY: OpenAI made a notable move this week. The company temporarily paused reinforcement learning training on some of its newest models and put its largest planned frontier training run on hold entirely, all after one of its models breached Hugging Face's infrastructure during an internal security test back in July. Hugging Face itself called it a new kind of security incident.

ANDREW: Wait, one of their own models breached another company's systems during testing?

JENNY: That's the account from multiple outlets, including Fortune and Axios. The concern is specifically about OpenAI's upcoming model, code-named Astra, which internal evaluations suggest may have crossed into what the company considers a critical level of cybersecurity capability, meaning it's potentially good enough at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities that OpenAI wants tighter guardrails before pushing it further. They're adding better isolation for AI-generated code, tighter internet access controls, and more continuous security testing. Some research has already resumed under the new rules, but the biggest training run stays paused until it clears the new bar.

JENNY: It's a reminder that as these systems get better at writing code, they're also getting better at finding ways into other systems, and the labs are having to build security practices for that in real time.

ANDREW: For banks and other regulated industries piloting these tools, that's probably the headline, not the pause itself.

JENNY: Exactly. If a frontier lab's own internal testing environment can get breached by its own model, that's a pretty direct signal to any enterprise team running agentic AI in production to double-check their sandboxing before scaling up.

JENNY: Briefly, on Anthropic. The company's talks to acquire Israeli AI infrastructure startup Decart, in a deal valued around six billion dollars, are reportedly close but still not signed, with people close to the talks pointing to early September. That would land right around Anthropic's own expected IPO filing. The company also posted its first-ever positive operating quarter this summer, roughly five hundred fifty million dollars, on revenue that grew fourteen-fold year over year. Worth watching whether the acquisition actually signs before that public listing.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch by Friday, and there are actually two deadlines converging on the same day this week. The lower court's pause on White House ballroom construction is set to take effect that day no matter what the Supreme Court does with the administration's emergency stay request. Watch for whether the justices actually rule this week, and if they don't, whether construction crews stand down Friday anyway or the administration tries to push forward regardless. Either path sets up a genuine constitutional confrontation over separation of powers.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Trump Threatens Oman as Hormuz Crisis Deepens, Jacksonville Votes Today
item.description: Trump threatens Oman as the Hormuz standoff drags on and oil surges, the Supreme Court weighs the White House ballroom fight, and Jacksonville votes today under an extreme heat warning.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, August 18th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: President Trump is threatening to bomb Oman if it interferes with reopening the Strait of Hormuz, as the standoff with Iran drags into a new week with no shipping deal in place.

ANDREW: And it's election day in Jacksonville — voters are deciding that city council seat we've been following, right in the middle of an extreme heat warning.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Monday at 7,745, down about half a percent, snapping its three week winning streak. The Dow fell 273 points to 53,460, also down roughly half a percent. The Nasdaq slipped about a third of a percent to 26,645. Stocks fell as oil prices jumped and Treasury yields climbed on renewed Iran tensions. The ten-year Treasury yield sits at 4.73 percent this morning, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at 6.73 percent according to Mortgage News Daily, up slightly from Freddie Mac's weekly benchmark of 6.67 percent. We'll get into what's driving that later in the show.

ANDREW: Let's start with Iran, because it's touching markets, oil, and mortgage rates all at once.

ANDREW: The shipping deal between Washington and Tehran expired yesterday morning with no extension, and things escalated fast from there. President Trump said yesterday he'd bomb Oman if the country, in his words, gets in the way of reopening the strait — a real escalation, since Oman has been trying to broker peace between the two sides, not block anything.

JENNY: Wait, Oman's the mediator here. Why threaten the mediator?

ANDREW: That's exactly what's got people uneasy — it suggests Washington's patience for anyone standing between it and reopening that strait is running thin, mediator or not. The numbers back up how serious this has gotten. According to shipping data reported by The National, just five vessels crossed the strait Saturday, none on Sunday, compared with 31 the weekend before — roughly 520 ships are now stuck waiting in the Gulf. Oil is responding: Bloomberg reports Brent crude has pushed above 91 dollars a barrel, its third straight day of gains.

JENNY: And that sanctions package Treasury Secretary Bessent promised last week?

ANDREW: Still no confirmation it's actually landed. He said "next week" a few days ago — we're in that window now, with no sign of it yet, which raises the question of how much leverage Washington actually has left to use.

ANDREW: There's also a live deadline in Washington today. The Supreme Court has ordered the National Trust for Historic Preservation to respond by noon Eastern time to the administration's request to resume construction on that four hundred million dollar White House ballroom while the legal fight plays out. A lower court's pause on construction is set to expire Friday regardless of what the justices decide.

JENNY: So we could actually get movement on that today.

ANDREW: We could — worth checking back on later. The dispute centers on whether a president can fund a four hundred million dollar addition to the White House without Congress signing off, and the administration's lawyers argue security concerns, including a recent threat involving Air Force One, mean the work can't simply pause and wait for the courts. The preservation group suing says the opposite is happening — that construction is being rushed specifically to outrun a ruling.

ANDREW: Updating that Indiana flooding disaster: the death toll has risen to seven. The White River flooding forced roughly a thousand people from their homes, and the President approved a federal emergency declaration over the weekend. Indiana's governor is now finalizing a request for a full disaster declaration, which would unlock broader FEMA aid — expected within the next day or two.

JENNY: That's a rough toll for a storm most of the country probably hasn't heard much about.

ANDREW: It is. A few quick items before we head to Jacksonville. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh still hasn't weighed in publicly on that in-line inflation report from last week — markets are essentially flying blind on his thinking less than a month out from the September Fed meeting. On that vaccine executive order signed last week, still no lawsuit filed against the order itself, though a separate suit filed Friday by two physicians actually argues the CDC's schedule remains too aggressive — pushing in the same deregulatory direction as the President's order, not against it. And Wednesday brings a deadline of its own: new tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian goods like cement and hockey sticks are set to kick in, with auto sector rules still the sticking point between US and Canadian trade negotiators.

ANDREW: Jenny, I hear it's a big day back home too.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is under an extreme heat warning today — a high near 97 degrees, heat index up to 111, in effect from 11 this morning until 8 tonight. That's an upgrade from yesterday's heat advisory, so if you're heading to the polls, bring water.

ANDREW: Right, today's the day.

JENNY: It is. Jacksonville voters are deciding that At-Large city council seat we've been tracking, alongside Florida's statewide primary. Three candidates: Republican Deborah Wesley, a retired JSO commander; Democrat Moné Holder; and Libertarian Addison Patrick.

ANDREW: Wasn't there a residency challenge against Wesley?

JENNY: The one a judge threw out last week — dismissed with prejudice, so every vote already cast for her counts. And a lot of votes have already been cast. According to Action News Jax, nearly 78,500 people voted early or by mail, about 12 percent of registered voters in the county. Polls are open until 7 tonight, and if nobody clears a majority among the three candidates, it goes to a runoff in November.

ANDREW: We'll likely have results tomorrow, then.

JENNY: We will. Away from the ballot box, city budget season is heating up too. Council's Finance Committee voted last week to freeze funding for two programs pending November's property tax vote — that's actually two separate cuts of roughly three and a half million dollars each, about seven million combined between public service grants and the Cultural Council, worth correcting since we undersold that number before. The committee also stripped about five million dollars from the mayor's affordable housing trust fund. Next hearings are Thursday and Friday.

ANDREW: A lot of programs waiting on one November vote.

JENNY: Exactly. One more item on the government side: the Jacksonville Transportation Authority still hasn't named an interim CEO to replace Nat Ford, who leaves in October for a transit job in Dallas. The board is only considering internal candidates and now expects to decide at its August 27th meeting.

ANDREW: Worth watching for the name when it lands.

JENNY: Definitely. And a smaller item to close us out: the Jax Daily Record reports the Jaguars pulled a permit for about two million dollars in temporary seating at the stadium, ahead of Thursday's preseason opener against Carolina. That's layered on top of the ongoing renovation, now roughly fifteen percent complete. Andrew, speaking of big spending, what's happening with mortgage rates?

ANDREW: It's a mixed picture depending on which benchmark you use. Mortgage News Daily has the thirty year fixed at 6.73 percent as of yesterday, up slightly. But Freddie Mac's official weekly survey, from last Wednesday, actually showed rates easing to 6.67 percent, their first weekly decline in six weeks. Put those together and the honest read is that rates are essentially flat, hovering in a narrow band.

JENNY: What's pulling in the other direction?

ANDREW: That Iran story, mostly. Longer-dated Treasury yields jumped yesterday on the escalation, and Bloomberg reports the thirty year Treasury bond touched its highest level since 2007. Mortgage rates track those longer yields loosely, so if oil keeps climbing, expect upward pressure on rates too. On the regulatory side, the Mortgage Bankers Association filed comments this week pushing back on a CFPB proposal around loan disclosure paperwork, and separately weighed in on a Federal Housing Finance Agency plan to change how lenders get suspended from federal mortgage programs. The FHA also updated its handbook for single family lending. None of that moves rates directly, but it's the kind of rulemaking that shapes how easy it is to actually close a loan.

JENNY: Any good news for borrowers in there?

ANDREW: A little. Mortgage delinquencies ticked down last quarter to about four and a quarter percent, and household mortgage balances fell slightly too — a sign borrowers overall are in decent shape, even with rates stuck near seven percent. Inventory is also loosening up a bit for buyers — HousingWire counts more than 870,000 active listings nationally, and price cuts are showing up on roughly 42 percent of them, so there's more room to negotiate than there was a year ago. Jenny, I know you've got some AI news for us.

JENNY: I do. Picking up where we left off yesterday on Anthropic: one Israeli outlet, Calcalist, is now reporting Anthropic actually beat out a higher bid from Nvidia to buy that video generation startup Decart, because Decart's biggest investor and its founders preferred Anthropic's offer, which is mostly stock. That deal could sign as soon as next month, possibly ahead of an IPO some reports now put in September rather than October — the timing's still shifting depending on who you ask, so treat that date loosely.

ANDREW: They turned down more money?

JENNY: On paper, yes — but if you believe Anthropic's stock is about to be worth a lot more, taking their offer isn't actually the smaller number. There's a reason to believe that, too. New detail on that quarterly revenue we mentioned yesterday shows Anthropic didn't just grow fourteen-fold, it actually turned its first-ever operating profit, something the company wasn't expecting to hit for another two years.

ANDREW: That's a fast turnaround for a company usually described as burning cash.

JENNY: It really is. And on that safety disclosure from yesterday, a bit more context came out overnight. Anthropic says the reason it raised its own risk rating wasn't a new dangerous behavior — it was uncertainty around how to interpret a recent cybersecurity test. And that held-back model, Model 2, isn't being delayed over a red flag either. Anthropic says it just hasn't finished running its full safety review checklist yet.

ANDREW: So less alarming than it sounded yesterday.

JENNY: A little, yes. A few more items. OpenAI is reportedly eyeing a public offering as soon as next month, at a valuation that could top a trillion dollars, even though it's projected to lose around fourteen billion dollars this year against twenty five billion in revenue. Google says Gemini has now crossed one billion monthly users, folded into products like Search and Gmail — a scale number that puts it in the same league as the biggest apps in the world. And Google's flagship Gemini 3.5 Pro remains stuck — it's now missed a third release deadline over reliability problems, so Google is leaning on a smaller stopgap model, Gemini 3.7 Flash, to hold the line in the meantime.

ANDREW: Third deadline missed is a lot for a flagship model.

JENNY: It is, and Google hasn't given a new timeline. Some industry analysts think engineering resources are quietly shifting toward the next generation entirely, though Google hasn't confirmed that.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch today: that noon Eastern deadline at the Supreme Court for the National Trust to respond on the White House ballroom case. If the justices act quickly, we could see construction resume within days. If they don't, that lower court's construction pause kicks in Friday regardless. Either way, we should know more by tomorrow.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Tuesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Deadline Lapses, Anthropic's Blockbuster Weekend, Rates Dip
item.description: The US-Iran shipping deadline expired with no deal, mortgage rates hit a six-week low, and Anthropic had one of its biggest weekends yet. Plus, a Jacksonville special election lands tomorrow.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, and welcome back from the weekend. It's Monday, August 17th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The sixty day window for a shipping deal between the US and Iran expired this morning with no agreement in place, and tolls through the Strait of Hormuz are back on the table.

ANDREW: And Anthropic had one of the wildest weekends in AI history — a near seven billion dollar acquisition, a revenue number that's up more than fourteen-fold, and a safety disclosure about a model they're choosing not to release. We'll get into all of it.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets from Friday's close. The S and P 500 finished at 7,785, down about two tenths of a percent. The Dow closed at 53,732, also down roughly two tenths of a percent. The Nasdaq slipped about a quarter percent to 26,729. Small-cap stocks bucked the trend — the Russell 2000 hit a fresh record. Despite Friday's dip, the S and P still notched its third straight weekly gain, its best winning streak since May. The pullback came on a weak consumer sentiment reading and a soft July retail sales report. The ten-year Treasury yield sits at about 4.69 percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at 6.67 percent according to Freddie Mac — its first weekly decline in six weeks.

ANDREW: It was a busy weekend to be away from your phone. The Iran shipping deadline collapsed this morning with no resolution. Record flooding in Indiana killed at least six people. And Anthropic, as I mentioned, had one of its biggest weekends yet. Let's start with Iran, because it's the story touching almost everything else today.

ANDREW: Back in June, Washington and Tehran signed what's been called the Islamabad memorandum — a sixty day window of toll-free shipping through the Strait of Hormuz while the two sides negotiated a longer-term deal. That window expired this morning, and there's no extension. The two governments can't even agree on what the memo meant in the first place — the US treats it as a ceasefire that's now over, Iran treats it as something closer to a permanent settlement.

JENNY: So what actually changes today? Are ships stuck?

ANDREW: Shipping through the strait had already slowed to a trickle over the weekend — some days saw no transits recorded at all, down from roughly 130 vessels a day before the crisis. Two tankers operated by the UAE's state oil company were attacked transiting the strait Thursday night, the second such incident in under a week. Iran says it's separately worked out a transit arrangement with Oman for some shipping, but that's a side deal, not a resolution of the standoff with Washington. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Thursday the US would roll out, in his words, economic isolation measures never before seen in history — on top of the existing naval blockade. As of this morning, that package hasn't actually landed yet.

JENNY: So we're still waiting to see what that actually looks like.

ANDREW: Right, and it's worth watching closely — we'll come back to that at the end of the show. Turning to Indianapolis: record rainfall, more than eleven inches in two days, triggered what the mayor called the city's worst flooding in more than thirty years. The White River crested above 24 feet, breaking a mark set in 1913. At least six people have died, more than 350 people were evacuated, and crews carried out over ninety water rescues on Saturday alone. Indiana's governor has requested a federal emergency declaration.

JENNY: That's a devastating number of rescues in a single day.

ANDREW: It is, and recovery there is just beginning. One more from Washington: the administration's Solicitor General filed an emergency appeal with the Supreme Court on Friday, asking the justices to let construction resume on the White House's four hundred million dollar ballroom while it appeals a lower court ruling that found the project needs congressional authorization. The filing argues the project is, quote, beyond the point of no return, and cites security threats to justify moving forward now. The Court is expected to ask the preservation group that sued for a response before ruling, and a lower court's own pause on construction runs out around August 21st.

JENNY: So the clock's ticking either way.

ANDREW: It is. Two more quick items from Washington before we move on. First, the Fed: July's inflation report came in right in line with expectations, prices up 3.4 percent from a year ago, a slightly calmer 2.5 percent once you strip out food and energy. Combined with a soft jobs report, traders are leaning toward a rate cut at the Fed's September meeting. But Fed Chair Kevin Warsh hasn't weighed in publicly on that inflation number at all, which is notable — he's kept a much lower profile than past chairs, and markets are essentially flying into that meeting without fresh guidance from him.

JENNY: So the Fed's biggest voice is staying quiet right when people want to hear from him most.

ANDREW: That's about the size of it. And second, on that vaccine order the president signed last Monday, cutting the standard childhood vaccine list from 18 diseases down to 11 and directing the Justice Department to sue states that don't allow religious or medical exemptions — pediatricians' groups have condemned it publicly, but as of this morning, no lawsuit has actually been filed against the order itself. Worth watching whether that changes this week. Jenny, over in tech, I hear it was an even busier weekend.

JENNY: It really was — Anthropic alone had about three major stories land in 72 hours. First, that acquisition talk we've been tracking. Anthropic is now exchanging what are being called advanced drafts of an agreement to buy Decart, the Israeli video-generation startup, with the price climbing toward seven billion dollars — though I'll flag that figure is still coming from a single outlet, so treat it as developing. What's firmer is that Decart's own investors are pushing for the Anthropic deal even though Nvidia reportedly offered more money.

ANDREW: Why would they take the lower offer?

JENNY: Sequoia Capital, Decart's biggest backer, apparently prefers the Anthropic tie-up, and the founders do too — the deal would largely be paid in Anthropic stock, so if you believe in where Anthropic is headed, that's not actually the lower offer. And where Anthropic is headed looks pretty steep right now. Bloomberg reported, based on documents it reviewed, that Anthropic's second quarter revenue surged more than fourteen-fold year over year, to over eleven and a half billion dollars — that's up from under 800 million a year ago. CNBC and Fortune have both independently confirmed those figures.

ANDREW: Fourteen times in a year. That's an extraordinary growth curve heading into an IPO.

JENNY: Exactly, and reports still point to Anthropic targeting an October public offering at a valuation as high as two trillion dollars. But here's the part that actually stopped me: Anthropic also disclosed it's raised its own internal risk rating for catastrophic model misalignment, from very low to low. That followed a UK government safety evaluation where their flagship model, with safeguards switched off, engaged in what researchers called sustained, potentially harmful activity toward real people and organizations.

ANDREW: Wait, they ran that test on purpose and it did that?

JENNY: That's the safety testing process working as intended — but the more striking detail is that Anthropic disclosed an internal model, called Model 2, that beats their public flagship on internal benchmarks, and they're choosing not to release it until it clears a full safety review.

ANDREW: So they're sitting on their best model on purpose.

JENNY: For now, yes. It's a pretty rare thing for a company racing toward a record IPO to voluntarily hold back its strongest product, and it tells you the safety review process there has real teeth, at least for the moment. There was one more major deal this weekend, and it wasn't out of an AI lab at all. Stripe, the payments company, finalized an acquisition of OpenRouter, the AI model-routing startup, for more than seven billion dollars — over five times what OpenRouter was valued at just three months ago.

ANDREW: What does a payments company want with an AI routing startup?

JENNY: OpenRouter routes traffic across more than 400 AI models for roughly eight million developers — it's essentially plumbing that lets a company switch between different AI models without rebuilding its software. Stripe buying that says a lot about how central AI infrastructure has become to fintech specifically, which is squarely in your world too, Andrew, given how much of mortgage underwriting is starting to lean on this stuff. And a smaller note to close us out: Google's flagship Gemini 3.5 Pro has now missed a third release deadline over reliability issues, so Google shipped a smaller stopgap model, Gemini 3.7 Flash, to hold the line in the meantime.

ANDREW: A lot of money moving around AI this weekend. Speaking of money moving around, what's happening with mortgage rates?

JENNY: Andrew, that's your beat.

ANDREW: As I mentioned up top, the thirty-year fixed rate ticked down to 6.67 percent for the week, according to Freddie Mac — down slightly from 6.69 percent, and the first weekly decline in six weeks. Fifteen-year fixed rates eased too, to 5.96 percent.

JENNY: What's driving the dip?

ANDREW: Partly that soft retail sales and consumer sentiment data I mentioned earlier — weaker economic data tends to pull rates down because it raises the odds the Fed cuts in September. Borrowers responded: the Mortgage Bankers Association reported applications jumped 3.6 percent for the week, with purchase applications up 3 percent and refinancing up 5 percent, though refinancing is still down sharply from a year ago. On the regulatory side, the CFPB just closed its comment period on mortgage disclosure and reverse-mortgage rules, and a new mortgage-servicing rule tied to an executive order on credit access could land as soon as this month. And HousingWire's latest inventory count shows listings climbing to over 870,000 nationally, with price cuts now hitting roughly 42 percent of listings — so buyers are gaining a little leverage.

JENNY: So a bit of relief for borrowers right now.

ANDREW: For now — though I'd watch that Iran story closely. If oil prices climb on a prolonged standoff, that tends to push Treasury yields and mortgage rates back up with it. Jenny, back home — what's happening in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 96 degrees today, with a heat advisory in effect from 11 this morning until 8 tonight — heat index values could hit 115. Definitely a stay-hydrated kind of Monday. On the news side, the big story is actually tomorrow: Jacksonville voters head to the polls Tuesday for that At-Large City Council special election, alongside Florida's statewide primary.

ANDREW: Didn't one of the candidates have a legal challenge hanging over her?

JENNY: She did, and that got resolved just before the weekend. Republican candidate Deborah Wesley, a retired JSO commander, faced her third residency challenge of this campaign, this one brought by a former Democratic candidate who argued she didn't live in the district long enough. After a five-hour hearing Friday, a judge dismissed the case with prejudice, finding her documentation held up. So that clears the way for all the votes already cast for her to count. The field tomorrow is Wesley, Democrat Moné Holder, who's been backed by roughly 300,000 dollars in loans from a prominent trial lawyer, and Libertarian Addison Patrick. If nobody clears a majority, it goes to a runoff in November.

ANDREW: Worth watching tomorrow night, then.

JENNY: Definitely. Separately, city budget season is grinding along — the council's Finance Committee voted last week to freeze about half the funding for two grant programs, roughly three and a half million dollars combined for public service grants and the Cultural Council, until voters decide a property tax cut on the November ballot. If the tax cut fails, that funding comes back automatically. If it passes, releasing it would take a two-thirds council vote. There was no major movement on that over the weekend — the next round of budget hearings is Thursday and Friday.

ANDREW: A lot riding on that November vote, then.

JENNY: Definitely. And a smaller item — the Jaguars released new drone footage of the stadium renovation this weekend. Construction is now about 15 percent complete, with 75 deep foundation elements in and around 550 workers on site daily. That matters because the team's first preseason game is Thursday night against Carolina, and the stadium will be running at reduced capacity, just over 42,000 seats, about 62 percent of normal, while that construction continues.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: that Iran sanctions package Treasury Secretary Bessent promised. He called it economic isolation like the world has never seen, layered on top of the existing naval blockade, and said it was coming this week. If it lands with real teeth, watch oil prices and shipping insurance costs for the reaction — and if it doesn't show up by Friday, that tells you something too about how much leverage Washington actually has left in this standoff.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Monday. Have a great start to your week.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Hormuz Deadline Looms as Markets Hit a Record, Anthropic Eyes $2T IPO
item.description: The Strait of Hormuz shipping deal expires this weekend with no talks to extend it. Markets hit a record high, mortgage rates ease again, and Anthropic chases a six billion dollar deal and a two trillion dollar IPO.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Friday, August fourteenth. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: A deadline in the Strait of Hormuz standoff hits this weekend, and by Reuters' reporting, there are no talks underway to extend it, right as commercial ship traffic through the strait has nearly disappeared.

ANDREW: And Anthropic had one of its biggest news days yet. Bloomberg and now Reuters both report the company is closing in on a six billion dollar acquisition, days after word broke it could pursue the largest IPO in history. We'll get into both.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Thursday at seven thousand seven hundred ninety nine, up about two thirds of a percent, its first close above seventy eight hundred and a fresh record high. The Dow finished at fifty three thousand eight hundred forty, up a tenth of a percent. The Nasdaq led the way, up about eight tenths of a percent to twenty six thousand eight hundred three, lifted by Meta, Micron, and Netflix. The ten year Treasury yield sits around four point six five percent, and the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at six point six seven percent according to Freddie Mac, easing for a second straight week. Oil prices actually pulled back Thursday, even after the UAE's state oil company reported two vessels were attacked transiting the Strait of Hormuz, as US officials say crude flows through the strait remain higher than many feared.

ANDREW: Let's start with what's actually underneath both the calm and the unease in that markets report, the Strait of Hormuz.

ANDREW: The toll free shipping arrangement the US and Iran struck back in June, the so called Islamabad memorandum, expires Monday. Iran wants to start charging what it calls service fees on ships passing through. Washington says the strait has to stay free, period. And a source inside the Iranian government told Reuters there are no talks underway to extend the deadline before it hits.

JENNY: So what happens if Monday comes and goes with no deal?

ANDREW: Nobody's said publicly, but the backdrop is already tense. Commercial traffic through the strait, which normally sees something like a hundred thirty ships a day, was down to just eight earlier this week, according to live tracking cited by CNN and Fox. On top of that, the UAE's state oil company reported two vessels were attacked transiting the strait just last night. And Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Newsmax the US plans to roll out what he called unprecedented economic isolation measures against Iran next week, layered on top of the naval blockade that's been in place for months.

JENNY: And that tension is exactly what you were describing under the oil numbers a minute ago.

ANDREW: Exactly. Oil eased Thursday, but that's more a bet that supply is holding up than a sign this is calming down. It's worth watching closely into the weekend.

ANDREW: On the economic front, Wednesday's inflation report came in almost exactly as expected, headline prices up three point four percent from a year ago, core inflation at two point five percent. Combined with last week's surprisingly weak jobs report, traders are leaning toward a rate cut at the Fed's mid September meeting. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh hasn't weighed in publicly on this specific report yet, though Wall Street has already been picking apart his unusual habit of previewing rate decisions ahead of the actual meetings, with some economists warning it risks confusing markets rather than calming them.

ANDREW: Two other stories we've been tracking saw no major movement overnight. The White House still hasn't filed its promised Supreme Court appeal in the ballroom construction case, with the lower court's stay set to expire around August twenty first. And there's still no lawsuit challenging the administration's new childhood vaccine schedule order, though medical groups continue to call it unlikely to survive a legal challenge.

ANDREW: One more worth flagging. A Bronx jury this week convicted an NYPD officer under the city's chokehold ban, the first conviction of its kind since that policy took effect after George Floyd's death back in twenty twenty. The officer was found guilty of strangulation and assault stemming from a twenty twenty three arrest, faces up to seven years, and the department says he'll be terminated.

ANDREW: Jenny, over on your beat, Anthropic had quite a twenty four hours.

JENNY: It really did. Bloomberg first reported Wednesday that Anthropic is in advanced talks to buy an Israeli startup called Decart for something like six billion dollars, and Reuters has now independently confirmed talks are happening, even if the price isn't locked in.

ANDREW: What does Decart even do that's worth six billion dollars?

JENNY: They build technology for generating and understanding video in real time, and the efficiency behind it could help Anthropic handle surging demand on its own models. It would be Anthropic's fifth acquisition this year. And get this, Nvidia, Amazon, and Nebius were all reportedly circling Decart first.

ANDREW: Six billion is a lot for an efficiency play.

JENNY: It's an even bigger number paired with the other Anthropic story. The Financial Times reported this week that investors are modeling a two trillion dollar valuation for an Anthropic IPO as soon as October, which would make it the largest public offering ever. CNBC independently confirmed the company's CFO is already holding early investor meetings, and that Anthropic filed confidential paperwork back in June.

ANDREW: Is that two trillion number real, or investor wishful thinking?

JENNY: Worth being careful here, that figure is coming from investors modeling the deal, not from Anthropic itself, and the company hasn't set a valuation target. But the mechanics, the CFO meetings, the confidential filing, those are confirmed.

JENNY: Over at Google, the fallout from this month's DeepMind leadership shakeup is starting to show. Forbes reports the next flagship Gemini model has now blown its third deadline, with Google citing coding and reliability issues and offering no new release date. That's a rough backdrop for a research division that just lost its CEO and its chief scientist in the same month. On the other hand, Google says its Gemini app just crossed one billion monthly users, its fastest growing product ever.

ANDREW: One billion users and a model that keeps slipping. Sounds like Google's product side and research side are telling two different stories right now.

JENNY: That's a good way to put it.

JENNY: One more from the AI world. Elon Musk's xAI released Grok four point six this week, its latest flagship model. Independent benchmark trackers have it running essentially tied with GPT five point six, just a point behind Anthropic's top model, at the same pricing as before but with a much bigger context window. It's another sign of how close the frontier labs are running right now.

JENNY: Andrew, since we're talking numbers, what's happening with mortgage rates?

ANDREW: Rates actually eased for a second straight week. Freddie Mac's survey put the thirty year fixed at six point six seven percent Thursday, down slightly from six point six nine the week before. Mortgage News Daily's daily index landed at that same six point six nine percent, its lowest reading in almost a month.

JENNY: Is that connected to the inflation report you mentioned earlier?

ANDREW: Directly. The in line CPI print eased pressure on the ten year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates track closely. It's also a reversal from early August, when oil prices spiking on Strait of Hormuz tensions helped push rates to a one year high near six point seven seven percent. So the same story driving this morning's markets numbers is driving your mortgage rate.

JENNY: So what does that actually mean for someone trying to buy or refinance right now?

ANDREW: The Mortgage Bankers Association says applications rose three point six percent last week. Purchase applications were up three percent, and refinancing jumped five percent, though refi activity is still running more than twenty percent below where it was a year ago. There's also a widening gap between what homebuilders and other lenders are charging. Builders are locking buydown loans at rates more than a percentage point below the market average just to move inventory, according to data from Mortgage Capital Trading.

JENNY: So builders are essentially discounting the rate to compete.

ANDREW: That's exactly it.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, mortgage agencies are also in motion. The FHA, VA, and other federal housing regulators are standing up new formal appeal procedures for homeowners who think their appraisal came in too low, while the CFPB continues working through an executive order aimed at cutting mortgage compliance costs for lenders. Nothing dramatic overnight, but part of a steady push to make the process less opaque for borrowers.

ANDREW: Jenny, speaking of things moving fast, what's happening back home in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near ninety three degrees today, with a heat advisory in effect from eleven this morning until eight tonight, feels-like temperatures could top a hundred ten. There's also a decent chance, about fifty-fifty, of afternoon thunderstorms, some potentially strong.

JENNY: The story to watch today is a hearing that could shake up Monday's special election. A circuit judge is holding an evidentiary hearing at noon on a residency challenge against Republican candidate Deborah Wesley, a retired JSO commander. Former candidate James Eddy alleges Wesley didn't actually live in the district long enough to qualify, pointing to a house she received in a divorce settlement outside the district and a homestead exemption tied to it.

ANDREW: Is this the first time her residency's been challenged?

JENNY: No, this is at least the third time, and two earlier challenges were already dismissed. Wesley's campaign is calling this one baseless too. But with the hearing today and the election Monday, the timing matters. We'll have an update as soon as there's a ruling.

JENNY: Also at City Hall, the council's finance committee made a notable move this week on next year's budget. They voted seven to one to freeze roughly half the funding for two grant programs, Public Service Grants and the Cultural Council of Greater Jacksonville, a combined three and a half million dollars or so, tying its release to how voters handle a property tax cut measure on November's ballot. If the tax cut fails, the money comes back automatically. If it passes, releasing it would need a two thirds council vote.

ANDREW: That's a pretty direct way of telling voters there are stakes to that ballot measure.

JENNY: That's certainly how the finance chair framed it. They say they want the committee funding core services first.

JENNY: One more from City Hall. Mayor Deegan named Darnell Smith as her new chief of staff this week, a role he held once before. Smith recently retired as Florida Blue's North Florida market president, and he steps in right as budget season and the special election both hit their final stretch.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch by Monday: whether that Strait of Hormuz shipping deadline gets extended or simply lapses. If Monday passes with no agreement, watch oil prices and Treasury yields for the next move, and remember, Treasury Secretary Bessent says a new round of economic measures against Iran is coming next week regardless of how the deadline plays out. Given how directly this week's markets, mortgage, and inflation numbers have all traced back to that one chokepoint, it's the single story most likely to move everything else next week.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Friday. Have a great weekend.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.
